title: The Harbor Petition
subtitle: Civic Research at the Waterfront
summary: Neighbors in the fictional Baltimore harbor community of Brewer's Wharf have petitioned against a 640-space garage on the last open shoreline lot. Listen to the public hearing, read the petition and survey, choose more evidence, and argue for a plan.

briefing.scene: In Brewer's Wharf, a fictional harbor neighborhood in Baltimore, the city has proposed a 640-space garage on the vacant Pier 9 lot. Residents have collected 1,240 signatures asking for a park instead. The City Planning Commission votes soon, and you are the Community Researcher who must understand every side.
briefing.goal: Gather and weigh evidence from a hearing, a petition and a survey, then recommend what should be built at Pier 9.

turns.speaker: Chair Brooks
turns.text: Good evening. This is the public hearing on the Pier 9 lot in Brewer's Wharf. Each speaker has two minutes. The commission has received a petition with 1,240 signatures. First, Ms. Collins.

turns.speaker: Ms. Collins
turns.text: Thank you. I have lived on Wharf Street for nineteen years. Our survey of 412 households found that only 18 percent want a parking garage, while 41 percent want a waterfront park. The lot floods at high tide, and a garage would cover the last open shoreline in our neighborhood. Parking already exists three blocks away, at the Dock Street lot.

turns.speaker: Mr. Nakamura
turns.text: Thank you, Chair. I run the water-taxi dock on the east pier. On festival weekends my boats turn away about 200 riders because there is nowhere for visitors to park. A garage would bring customers to our restaurants and shops. I agree with the neighbors about flooding, so I ask the commission to require a raised first floor and a rain garden on the roof.

turns.speaker: Chair Brooks
turns.text: Thank you both. Written comments are due by April 2, and the commission will vote on April 9. This hearing is adjourned.

petition.title: Petition to the City Planning Commission, Brewer's Wharf residents
text: To the Members of the City Planning Commission:
We, the undersigned residents and workers of Brewer's Wharf, respectfully submit this petition about the use of the vacant Pier 9 lot.

Whereas the Pier 9 lot is the last open shoreline in our neighborhood; and whereas high-tide flooding covered the lot on 14 days in 2025; and whereas a survey of 412 households found that 18 percent support a parking garage and 41 percent support a waterfront park; and whereas the Dock Street lot, three blocks away, already provides 220 parking spaces;
Therefore, we respectfully request that the Commission reject the proposed 640-space garage and instead fund a waterfront park, a water-taxi landing, and a covered bus shelter.
This petition carries 1,240 signatures. Submitted March 3.

field-notes.title: Researcher's Field Notes: The East Dock
text: Field notes, Saturday, July 12, east dock. I stood at the dock from 2:00 to 3:00 p.m. and counted 126 riders. Of the 126 riders I counted, 41 said they came by bus.
The bus stops three blocks from the dock and has no shelter. Eleven people left the line because it started to rain and there was nowhere dry to wait.
field-notes.summary: A researcher counted 126 riders at the east dock; 41 came by bus, the bus stop has no shelter, and 11 people left the line when it rained.

phases.title: Public Hearing: Pier 9
phases.instructions: Listen to part of the public hearing. Three people speak. Listen for each person's position and the reasons they give.

tasks.q: What is Ms. Collins's main reason for opposing the garage?

options.text: A garage would cost the city too much money to build and run.
Parking cannot be built anywhere except three blocks away.
Garages are always bad for every neighborhood in the city.
A garage would cover the last open shoreline and the lot floods.

tasks.explain: Ms. Collins says the lot 'floods at high tide' and that a garage 'would cover the last open shoreline in our neighborhood.' She does not mention cost, and she says parking already exists nearby, not that it can only be built there.

tasks.q: How does Mr. Nakamura's position differ from Ms. Collins's?

options.text: He accepts a garage if it is built to handle flooding.
He says the neighbors are wrong that the lot floods.
He runs the water-taxi dock on the east pier of the harbor.
He wants the commission to cancel the vote and start over.

tasks.explain: Mr. Nakamura says he agrees about flooding, then asks for a raised first floor and a rain garden. So he accepts a garage with conditions. His job is true but does not answer how the positions differ.

tasks.q: Choose the statements that support the claim: 'Residents have strong reasons to ask for a park.'

pool.text: only 18 percent want a parking garage, while 41 percent want a waterfront park
The lot floods at high tide
Parking already exists three blocks away, at the Dock Street lot.
my boats turn away about 200 riders because there is nowhere for visitors to park
I have lived on Wharf Street for nineteen years.
the commission will vote on April 9

phases.title: Primary Source: The Residents' Petition
phases.instructions: Read the petition and the survey table. Notice how the petition is organized and which evidence it uses.

tasks.q: What do the residents ask the Planning Commission to do?

options.text: Build a garage with a raised first floor and a rain garden.
Reject the garage and fund a park, water-taxi landing and bus shelter.
Move the harbor festival to a different neighborhood this year.
Close the Dock Street lot and turn it into new housing units.

tasks.explain: The 'Therefore' paragraph asks the Commission to 'reject the proposed 640-space garage and instead fund a waterfront park, a water-taxi landing, and a covered bus shelter.' The raised first floor was Mr. Nakamura's idea, not the petition's.

tasks.q: Which statement is supported by the survey table?

options.text: More households chose the garage than the water-taxi landing and bus shelter.
Almost every household opposes any new building at Pier 9.
More households chose the waterfront park than any other option.

tasks.explain: The park has 168 households, the highest count. The garage has 74, fewer than the 109 for the water-taxi landing and bus shelter. The table does not show opposition to all building.

tasks.q: Why does the petition begin its reasons with the word 'Whereas'?

options.text: To ask the Commission a question about the vote.
To list reasons before stating the request.
To say that the garage has already been approved.
To show that the petition is only 14 days old.

tasks.explain: 'Whereas' introduces each fact or reason. The request begins at 'Therefore.' This is the formal order of a petition: reasons first, then the request.

tasks.q: How does the survey table strengthen the petition?

options.text: It proves that 1,240 people signed the petition.
It shows that every single neighbor wants a park built.
It shows that parking costs less than building a park.
It gives the counts behind the 18 percent garage figure.

tasks.explain: The petition says 18 percent support a garage. The table gives the counts behind that percent (74 of 412). The signatures come from the petition itself, not the survey.

tasks.q: Mr. Nakamura says visitors have nowhere to park. Which claim in the petition does his testimony challenge?

options.text: That visitors can use the Dock Street lot instead.
That 1,240 people signed the petition in March.
That the lot is the last open shoreline nearby.

tasks.explain: The petition lists the Dock Street lot's 220 spaces as a reason a garage is unnecessary. Mr. Nakamura says riders still cannot find parking, so he challenges that reason. The signature count and the shoreline claim are not about parking.

tasks.q: What can you infer from the petition's fact that the lot flooded on 14 days in 2025?

options.text: The city never plans for rain or storms in any project.
Flooding always stops on days when a festival is held.
The lot is not a safe place for paved parking.

tasks.explain: Frequent flooding makes a paved garage a risky use of the site, which is why the petition lists it as a reason. The text does not say anything about the city's planning in general or about festival days.

phases.title: Decide What Evidence to Gather
phases.instructions: Before the commission votes, you can collect one more kind of evidence. Choose one. Either choice leads to a complete mission.

decision.q: Which evidence do you gather before the vote?

options.text: Count cars on Wharf Street at 5 p.m.
options.consequence: The count shows that Wharf Street is already crowded on festival nights, which supports Mr. Nakamura's parking concern but also suggests a garage would add even more traffic.

board.label: Traffic count
board.text: Festival night: 1,180 cars per hour, nearly four times the weekday count of 310.

board.label: Traffic count
board.text: A 640-space garage would send more cars onto a street that is already crowded.

options.text: Interview riders at the water-taxi dock
options.consequence: Your field notes show that many riders already arrive by bus, which supports the residents' request for a bus shelter and challenges the idea that every visitor needs a parking space.

board.label: Field notes
board.text: Of 126 riders counted on a Saturday, 41 came by bus.

board.label: Field notes
board.text: Eleven people left the line when it rained because there was no shelter.

phases.title: Testify at the Hearing
phases.instructions: Give your two-minute testimony. Use the sources and the facts on your board.

task.title: Two Minutes at the Hearing
task.scenario: You are a Community Researcher giving testimony at the public hearing. You have one minute to persuade the Planning Commission about the Pier 9 lot.
task.prompt: State your position on the Pier 9 lot. Give two reasons using the survey and the petition. Then answer Mr. Nakamura's concern about parking in one or two sentences.

text: Survey of 412 households: 41 percent chose a waterfront park; 18 percent chose a parking garage.
Petition: the Dock Street lot, three blocks away, already provides 220 parking spaces. High-tide flooding covered the Pier 9 lot on 14 days in 2025.
Mr. Nakamura: 'On festival weekends my boats turn away about 200 riders because there is nowhere for visitors to park.'

frames: I believe the commission should ___ because ___.
First, the survey of ___ shows that ___.
Mr. Nakamura is right that ___, but ___.
guided.model: I believe the commission should build a waterfront park at Pier 9 because it matches what residents want. First, the survey of 412 households shows that 41 percent chose a park and only 18 percent chose a garage. Second, the petition states that the lot flooded on 14 days in 2025. Mr. Nakamura is right that visitors need parking, but the Dock Street lot, three blocks away, already has 220 spaces.

successCriteria: I state my position in my first sentence.
I use at least two numbers from the sources.
I use a signal word such as 'first' or 'second' to organize my reasons.
I answer the other side with 'but' or 'however'.

listenFor: Numbers connected to a reason, not just listed
A response that acknowledges Mr. Nakamura before disagreeing
teacher.followUp: Which fact from the sources was hardest for the other side to answer?

chose-traffic.promptAdd: Answer Mr. Nakamura with your Wharf Street count: say how busy the street is on festival nights and what a garage would add.

plannerHint.reply: Use the festival-night and weekday car counts to answer his parking concern.

chose-traffic.revisionPrompt: Does your reply use the car counts from Wharf Street? Did you compare festival night with a weekday?

chose-riders.promptAdd: Answer Mr. Nakamura with your dock interviews: say how many riders came by bus and what happened when it rained.

plannerHint.reply: Use your rider count and the bus numbers to answer his parking concern.

chose-riders.revisionPrompt: Does your reply use what you learned from the riders at the dock? Which number shows how they travel, and what does it say about parking?

task.title: Letter to the Commission

task.prompt: Write a letter that recommends what should be built at the Pier 9 lot. Use at least two pieces of evidence, and answer the strongest argument from the other side.

frames: Dear Commission members, I recommend that ___ because ___.
guided.model:
Dear Commission members, I recommend that Pier 9 become a waterfront park because it matches what residents want and fits the land. The survey of 412 households shows that 41 percent chose a park, while only 18 percent chose a garage. The petition also states that the lot flooded on 14 days in 2025.

Some people argue that visitors need parking. Mr. Nakamura says his boats turn away about 200 riders on festival weekends. However, the Dock Street lot, three blocks away, already has 220 spaces, so a shuttle or a bus shelter could connect visitors to the dock. Thank you for considering my letter.

revisionPrompts.prompt: Check each number. Did you say what it counts (households, days, spaces)?
After each piece of evidence, add 'This shows that ...' to explain why it matters.
Use a transition such as 'However' or 'On the other hand' to introduce the opposing view.

successCriteria: I state a clear recommendation in the first paragraph.
I use at least two numbers from the sources and say what they count.
I describe the opposing view fairly and respond to it.

lookFor: A claim that names a specific use for the lot
A fair summary of the opposing view before the reply
commonIssues: Listing numbers without explaining why they matter
Using informal opinion words instead of evidence

chose-riders.promptAdd: Use your dock interview notes as part of your answer to the other side. Include how many riders came by bus and what the rain changed.

plannerHint.counter: Answer the parking concern with the bus riders you counted.
plannerHint.ev2: Use your field notes as extra support, such as the bus shelter.

chose-riders.revisionPrompt: Does your answer to the other side use your rider notes? What do the bus numbers tell the commission about parking spaces?

teacherQuestions: Which piece of evidence changed your mind or strengthened your view the most, and why?
How did the extra evidence you chose (traffic count or rider interviews) change your argument?
How did you describe the other side fairly before you disagreed with it?
debrief.connections: Connect to civics: how residents use petitions, public hearings and written comments to take part in local decisions. Compare a primary source (the petition) with a spoken source (the hearing) and ask which gives stronger evidence and why.
